title: Conditional Independence
quickIdea: A and C are conditionally independent given B when P(A and C|B) = P(A|B)P(C|B). It is a different statement from independence, and neither direction of implication holds.
remember: The definition applies the product test inside the conditional measure: same test, different measure.
Independence does not survive conditioning. Two independent coins, given that at least one is a head, become dependent: 1/3 against the required 1/4.
Conditional independence does not give unconditional independence either; the eight-outcome construction on this card is a counterexample with all the numbers small.
Conditional independence is the assumption behind naive Bayes classifiers and behind 'the trials are independent given the parameter' in Bayesian statistics.
Check the product inside the condition. Computing P(A and C) and comparing it with P(A)P(C) answers a different question.
In GATE CSE 2026 Set 2 Q.53 the two events share a toss, so they are not independent; the answer still comes out as 1/2 because the shared trial is handled by counting, not by multiplying.

example.prompt: Two fair coins are tossed. A = head on the first, C = head on the second, B = at least one head. Test A and C for independence, then for conditional independence given B.
example.work: Unconditionally P(A and C) = 1/4 = (1/2)(1/2), so A and C are independent. Given B = {HH, HT, TH}, P(A|B) = 2/3, P(C|B) = 2/3 and P(A and C|B) = P(HH|B) = 1/3. The product (2/3)(2/3) = 4/9 is not 1/3, so they are conditionally dependent.
example.answer: Independent, but dependent given at least one head.

gateAngle: This is the concept behind the two hardest questions in the topic: GATE CSE 2015 Set 3 Q.37 (a function of the conditioned variable is constant given the condition) and GATE CSE 2026 Set 2 Q.53 (two events that share a toss). Neither is solved by assuming independence.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: With A, C independent and B = at least one head, what is P(A and C|B), and what would conditional independence require?
variations.why: The condition removes TT, which is the outcome that carried the independence; the remaining three outcomes favour agreement between the coins.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: Eight equally likely outcomes 1 to 8. B = {1,2,3,4}, A = {1,2}, C = {1,3,5,6,7,8}. Are A and C independent? Are they independent given B?
variations.why: P(A) = 1/4, P(C) = 3/4 and P(A and C) = 1/8, against a product of 3/16, so they are dependent. Inside B, P(A|B) = 1/2, P(C|B) = 1/2 and P(A and C|B) = 1/4, so the product holds.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: If A and C are conditionally independent given B and also given B^c, must they be independent?
variations.why: The eight-outcome construction above is independent given B and (degenerately) given B^c, yet dependent overall; mixing two measures can destroy the product.

trap.what: Assuming that independence is preserved when a condition is added, or that conditional independence implies independence.
trap.why: Conditioning replaces the measure, and a product that held under one measure has no reason to hold under another.
trap.counterexample: Two independent coins become dependent given at least one head: 1/3 against 4/9.

check.question: Two fair coins are tossed and at least one is a head. What is P(both heads | at least one head), and why is it not 1/2?
check.explanation: The surviving outcomes are HH, HT, TH. Only HH has both heads, so the probability is 1/3; 1/2 would be right only if the two coins stayed independent under the condition, which they do not.
